name: Kingston Creative
overview: Non-profit arts organisation that runs the Kingston Art District, centred on Water Lane in Downtown Kingston, and the Artwalk Festival (stated by Kingston Creative).

Founded in February 2017. Andrea Dempster Chung, now executive director, co-founded it with Alan Daisley and Jennifer Bailey (Jamaica Observer, 2024). Its first project was painting murals on Water Lane.

Site and buildings: no building of its own for the district, which is a set of streets. Its office and coworking space, Kingston Creative Space, is at 107 Harbour Street, upstairs at F&B Downtown, and was backed by the Development Bank of Jamaica and TEF (Jamaica Observer).
funding_verdict: Kingston Creative: donor-funded: development banks, Jamaican companies, foundations and grants

name: Benesse Art Site Naoshima
overview: The collective name for all art activities run by Benesse Corporation and the Fukutake Foundation on Naoshima and Teshima in Kagawa Prefecture and Inujima in Okayama Prefecture (stated by Benesse Art Site).

Benesse Corporation began on Naoshima in 1989 with a campsite, opened Benesse House, a hotel and art museum complex, in 1992, started the Art House Project in the Honmura district in 1998, and opened the Chichu Art Museum in 2004 (Mecenat, a Japanese corporate philanthropy association).

Soichiro Fukutake, Honorary Chairman of the Fukutake Foundation and General Producer of the Setouchi Triennale, began visiting Naoshima to continue his father's project of building a children's campsite there (stated by Benesse Art Site).
funding_verdict: Benesse Art Site Naoshima: corporate-funded: Benesse Corporation and the Fukutake family, now with private equity ownership
wider_context: In July 2014 Benesse Corporation announced a leak of customer personal data, with a maximum of about 20.7 million records; police began an investigation on 7 July (Gigazine, 9 July 2014). The Gigazine article does not mention Naoshima or the art site.
Benesse Corporation funds the art site; the leak concerns the company, not the museums.

name: Teshima Art Museum
overview: The Teshima Art Museum is at 607 Karato, Teshima, Tonosho-cho, Kagawa, and is one of the sites of Benesse Art Site Naoshima (museum page).

The page dates Rei Naito's permanent installation Matrix, housed in the museum, to 2010 and does not state an opening year; Ryue Nishizawa designed the building, a concrete shell without pillars (museum page).
What is there: one work, Matrix, in which water trickles from the ground throughout the day (museum page).
funding_verdict: Teshima Art Museum: the pages read name no funder; it sits within Benesse Art Site Naoshima

name: Amman Design Week
overview: Biennial design festival held across Amman. The 2026 edition ran from 2 to 17 October across Amman and, for the first time, Aqaba, with 59 participating spaces, 204 events and over 220 designers (Yanko Design, 30 September 2026).

Founded in 2016. The Jordan Times (30 August 2016) calls it an initiative of Queen Rania and says she conceived it. Yanko Design says she founded it. Earlier editions followed in 2017 and 2019. 2026 is the fourth, returning after seven years (Yanko Design).

Not tied to one building. The 2026 main exhibition is at the Ras El Ain Hangar, with other venues at Darat Abu Adnan in Jabal Al Lweibdeh, Iraq Al Amir including Qasr Al Abd, and Ayla Oasis in Aqaba (e-flux, 2026 edition).
funding_verdict: Amman Design Week: royal-patronage festival with a municipal partner and private sponsors

name: Circle Art Gallery
overview: Commercial gallery and art agency in Lavington, Nairobi, at Victoria Square, Riara Road (stated by the gallery).

Established in Nairobi in 2012. Its About page names Danda Jaroljmek, Arvind Vohora and Fiona Fox as founders and says the idea was born in 2013 in a converted 1970s house in Lavington. The sources give both years. Jaroljmek is the director.
In 2015 it built what it calls the first white cube gallery in Nairobi. In 2020 it joined Cromwell Place, a gallery membership club in London (stated by the gallery).
funding_verdict: Circle Art Gallery: privately owned company: a limited company with 15 named shareholders

name: Arab Image Foundation (AIF)
overview: Photography archive and research centre in Kantari, Beirut, holding roughly 500,000 photographic objects dating back to 1860 from South West Asia, North Africa and their diasporas (stated by the foundation). Wikipedia gives two figures, 500,000 and over 600,000.

Registered in Beirut as an independent association in 1997 (stated by the foundation). Founded by the photographers Fouad Elkoury and Samer Mohdad and the artist Akram Zaatari. Lucien Samaha was also an original member (Wikipedia).

Premises: moved to Kantari in 2023 from earlier premises in Gemmayze, used from 2011. The Kantari space has preservation, digitisation and research labs, a shared library, an auditorium and a public work and gathering space shared with partner organisations (stated by the foundation).
funding_verdict: Arab Image Foundation: foundation-funded: six funders named on its about page

press_items.title: Claudia Polledri, "The Arab Image Foundation through Akram Zaatari's Eyes: Or, Variations on the Theme of Photography" (issue 109, Spring-Summer 2018)

name: Ashkal Alwan
aliases: the lebanese association for plastic arts
overview: Non-profit for the plastic arts in Beirut, registered with Lebanon's Ministry of Interior and Municipalities under number 249/AD (stated on its site). Also known as the Lebanese Association for Plastic Arts.

Founded in 1994 by Christine Tohmé, Marwan Rechmaoui, Rania Tabbara, Mustapha Yamout and Leila Mroueh, after the Lebanese war (Wikipedia). The Sigrid Rausing Trust gives 1993, and Tohmé's 2012 Ibraaz interview mentions both years. Tohmé is its director.
Name means "forms and colours" in Arabic (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Ashkal Alwan: grant-funded: foreign foundations and a Norwegian ministry, plus private donors

press_items.title: Hicham Awad, "Navigating Volatility: Home Workspace Program at Ashkal Alwan" (2026)
Hrag Vartanian, "Lebanese Art Community Joins Unprecedented Protests" (2019)

name: Kunstmuseum Liechtenstein
aliases: Kunstmuseum Liechtenstein mit Hilti Art Foundation
overview: Liechtenstein's state museum of modern and contemporary art, at Städtle 32 in the pedestrian zone of Vaduz.
A gift of ten paintings to the state in 1967 led to the founding of the state art collection the following year, with Georg Malin as its first curator.
A group of private donors, the government and the municipality of Vaduz made the building possible. It was handed to the state in August 2000 and opened on 11 November 2000.
funding_verdict: Kunstmuseum Liechtenstein: public: the State of Liechtenstein pays four fifths of the budget

name: ILHAM Gallery
overview: Public art gallery for modern and contemporary art at Levels 3 and 5, Ilham Tower, No 8 Jalan Binjai, Kuala Lumpur (Art Rabbit; ILHAM Gallery website).

Founded in 2015. IB Tower Sdn Bhd ran the gallery and gift shop from 2015, and the non-profit Yayasan ILHAM, established on 22 October 2018, took over on 1 January 2019 (stated by the space, About page).

Gallery director Rahel Joseph describes it as a "privately-funded public art gallery" opened to fill an institutional gap in Kuala Lumpur (Art & Market, Rahel Joseph, "10 Years of ILHAM Gallery", 23 October 2025).
funding_verdict: ILHAM Gallery: privately funded, by the space's own description: run by the non-profit Yayasan ILHAM
wider_context: December 2023: the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) seized Ilham Tower under a notice dated 18 December 2023, addressed to the former finance minister Daim Zainuddin as owner. The Star reported that the tower is owned by Daim's family (The Star, Tarrence Tan, "Daim's Ilham Tower seized by MACC", 21 December 2023).

The Edge Malaysia Weekly tied the seizure to an MACC investigation, begun in May 2023, of the Renong Bhd and United Engineers Malaysia Bhd deal of the late 1990s that cost RM2.3 billion ("MACC moves in on Daim", issue of 25 to 31 December 2023).
Wikipedia names the owner as Ilham Tower Sdn Bhd, a majority-owned subsidiary of Ilham Baru Sdn Bhd, controlled by Daim's wife Na'imah Abdul Khalid and their two sons.

June 2025: the MACC seized the tower a second time under the Anti-Money Laundering Act 2001 (The Star, Benjamin Lee, "MACC seizes Ilham Tower again", 5 June 2025). The Vibes reported on 25 June 2025 that the MACC planned to file for forfeiture that day at the Kuala Lumpur High Court, and valued the tower at RM1.5 billion to RM2 billion ("MACC to file for Ilham Tower forfeiture today").
The gallery's address is Levels 3 and 5 of Ilham Tower (Art Rabbit), and the company that ran the gallery from 2015 to 2018, IB Tower Sdn Bhd, is listed by Wikipedia as the tower's developer.

name: Bikini Wax EPS
overview: Independent art project space run by a collective of artists, writers, poets and filmmakers in Mexico City. Sources spell the name "Biquini Wax EPS". The city's tourism site gives the address as Pedro de Alba 232, Iztaccihuatl, Benito Juárez. My Art Guides gives Lago Ayarza 22, Torre Blanca, Miguel Hidalgo.

Elephant (2019) names Daniel Aguilar Ruvalcaba as founder: he started it in 2011 at his grandmother's home in Guanajuato and moved it to Mexico City in 2013 when he went to study art. My Art Guides instead says artist Israel Urmeer founded it in 2008 in Heroica Zitácuaro, Michoacán, and that it has run in Mexico City since 2011.
Elephant describes a "contemporary art sect" with twelve members and no leader. Members do not show their own work in the space.
funding_verdict: Bikini Wax EPS: collectively run, with named backers

name: Cráter Invertido
overview: Artist cooperative that self-manages a multidisciplinary house-workshop in Mexico City with a risograph press and an experimental radio, among other tools for dialogue and self-publishing (stated by the space; Arts Collaboratory).

Its members are graduates of UNAM's National School of Visual Arts and of the "La Esmeralda" School of Painting, Sculpture and Printmaking (MUAC, UNAM); Time Out Mexico (2016) says the group formed at La Esmeralda under the name Grupo D.

Founding dates differ: the cooperative's own site and MUAC give 2011; Kunstinstituut Melly gives 2012 and places its archive space and publishing workshop in the Obrera neighbourhood. Time Out Mexico (29 February 2016) gave the address as Joaquín García Icazbalceta 32, colonia San Rafael, near Metro San Cosme.
funding_verdict: Cráter Invertido: member-run cooperative; its one named backer is the Arts Collaboratory network

name: SOMA
overview: Non-profit, non-commercial and non-governmental art school, residency and public talks platform in Mexico City. Since 2026 it occupies a house in the San Miguel Chapultepec neighbourhood (SOMA Summer 2025 listed the address as Alumnos 47, San Miguel Chapultepec, Miguel Hidalgo). Before that it was in San Pedro de los Pinos (e-flux, 2026).

Founded in 2009 when the artist Yoshua Okón convened a group of 19 artists (Wikipedia). Carla Herrera-Prats started the SOMA Summer course and it took its current form in 2011 (e-flux, 2015). Okón co-founded the earlier artist-run space La Panadería with Miguel Calderón and places SOMA in that tradition (Artillery, 2013).

Named by vote of its Artists Council, which included Francis Alÿs, Teresa Margolles, Mario García Torres and Julieta Aranda. Okón links the word to Aldous Huxley's use of it and to the Greek word for body (Artillery, 2013).
funding_verdict: SOMA: privately funded: donors, an annual benefit auction and a board of patrons, with no government money

press_items.title: Kim Córdova, "Fifteen years of SOMA: Why institutionality can be its own political act" (2026)
Matt Stromberg, "Independent Art Spaces Thrive in Mexico City" (15 April 2015)

name: National Art Museum of Moldova
overview: National art museum in central Chișinău, with its main building at 115 Strada 31 August 1989.

Founded in 1939 (museum website). Wikipedia names the sculptor Alexandru Plămădeală and the painter Auguste Baillayre as founders and gives 26 November 1939 as the date. The original collection came mostly from donations by Bessarabian artists, with works from the Ministry of Culture and Arts in Bucharest. The whole collection was moved to Kharkiv at the start of the war and disappeared there (museum website).

Building: the central Dadiani building was designed by Alexandru Bernardazzi and built in 1901 "with the funds of Princess Natalia Dadiani" as a girls' gymnasium. It later housed the Central Committee of the Communist Party of the Moldavian SSR and was handed to the museum in 1989. Three earthquakes in 1990 forced the central section to close (museum website).
funding_verdict: National Art Museum of Moldova: mainly public: the Moldovan state through the Ministry of Culture, with one-off Romanian state aid for the building
wider_context: A Court of Accounts audit of state budget spending in 2023 and 2024 found "significant deviations from the legal requirements" in how the Ministry of Culture and seven state museums managed money and cultural heritage, including unjustified expenditure and uncollected rent (Logos Press, 23 December 2025). Across the audited museums, only 0.38% of the 900,700 movable heritage units appear in accounting records.
The National Museum of Art is one of the seven museums audited; the article gives no separate findings for each museum.

name: Ulaanbaatar International Media Art Festival (UBIMAF)
overview: Festival of media art in Ulaanbaatar, run by the Arts Council of Mongolia (ACM), a non-governmental organisation. ACM states that it has organised the festival since 2015.
The first edition ran from 9 June to 9 July 2016 under the theme "Tradition and Modernity", with 18 artists from nine countries (ASEF Culture360).
ACM was established in 2002 by Mongolian arts, civic and business leaders supported by the Mongolian Foundation for an Open Society (Soros Foundation) (ASEF Culture360, 1 June 2017).
funding_verdict: Ulaanbaatar International Media Art Festival: NGO-run, funded by foreign cultural bodies and embassies; no funder list for later editions

press_items.title: Nominbileg P., "Losing and finding our reality | A review of Ulaanbaatar International Media Art Festival" (6 August 2020)

name: LE 18, Derb el Ferrane
overview: Independent art space and artist residency in the medina of Marrakech, at 18 Derb El Ferrane, with exhibitions, residencies, talks, workshops and the yearly publication "Chergui" (le18marrakech.com).
Opened in 2013 by Laila Hida, founder and director, with the curator Hicham Bouzid (le18marrakech.com; Contemporary And, Louise Thurin, 2 May 2023).
Building: a riad at 18 Derb el Ferrane whose rooms surround a courtyard open to the sky (e-flux, Jamila Moroder, 30 September 2022; le18marrakech.com).
funding_verdict: LE 18: independent, partner-funded: a structural patron, foundations, cultural institutes and embassies
wider_context: e-flux (Jamila Moroder, "Field Notes: Jamila Moroder on LE 18, Documenta 15", 30 September 2022) writes that a poster by Villalobos reflects "a clear distrust of Documenta as a state- and corporate-sponsored German institution," and quotes the ruangrupa members Reza Afisina and Farid Rakun calling the exhibition "almost a state affair."

The piece is a review of LE 18's contribution to documenta fifteen: LE 18 chose not to provide finished artworks for the opening after exhausting negotiations with documenta's bureaucracy, and showed leftovers and preparatory documentation in its relief center.

name: MACAAL
overview: Museum of African Contemporary Art Al Maaden (MACAAL, in French Musée d'Art Contemporain Africain Al Maaden) at Al Maaden, Sidi Youssef Ben Ali, Marrakech, on the other side of town from the Medina (macaal.org; The Art Newspaper).

Founded by the private collector Othman Lazraq with his father Alami Lazraq. The Art Newspaper dates its opening to 2018, Euronews and The National say it was created in 2016. Its first exhibition, "Africa Is No Island", opened alongside the first Marrakech 1-54 art fair (Galerie, The Art Newspaper). Fondation Alliances runs it. Lazraq is president of both (The National).
Named for the Al Maaden district where it sits.
funding_verdict: MACAAL: privately funded: the Lazraq family, through Fondation Alliances

press_items.title: Tom Seymour, "After 2023 earthquake, Marrakech's pioneering art museum reopens" (2025)
Florence Derieux, interview with Othman Lazraq (2025)

name: L'Appartement 22
overview: Independent, experimental contemporary art space at 279 avenue Mohamed V in Rabat, with exhibitions, workshops, symposia, residencies, a publishing line and a radio station (the space's website; Contemporary And).

Founded in 2002 (October 2002, according to Contemporary And) by the independent curator Abdellah Karroum. Gatherings began in summer 2002 in Karroum's own apartment, which overlooked the capital's main street. He turned his home into a space for research and action because Moroccan institutions did not prioritise this kind of work (Karroum, C&, 2013).
Building: an apartment, not a purpose-built space.
funding_verdict: L'Appartement 22: funders not published: no funder is named on its own site, and the only named supporters are for the founder's research

name: Associação Núcleo de Arte
overview: Artists' association in an old villa in the centre of Maputo (africaserver.nl profile). Globalnyt (29 December 2016) places it in the Polana Cimento neighbourhood near the Mercado do Museu.

The profile on africaserver.nl calls it the oldest artists' collective in Mozambique and gives 1948 as the "more official foundation". The name first appeared in 1937 as the title of an exhibition in Lourenço Marques that featured only Portuguese artists. Culturgest says Núcleo de Arte was founded in 1936 by the Portuguese painter Frederico Ayres. Globalnyt gives 1921.

Mozambican artists were gradually admitted. A 1964 exhibition of Malangatana's work, staged by the Núcleo dos Estudantes Africanos, was closed by the secret police. After independence in 1975 the group was renamed COAP and the Associação Núcleo de Arte name was later restored. It closed several times during the civil war and in the early 1990s, and in 1993 a group of young artists reopened the building (africaserver.nl).
funding_verdict: Associação Núcleo de Arte: member-run artists' association; the profile names Hivos as a donor

name: Franco-Namibian Cultural Centre (FNCC)
overview: French-Namibian cultural centre at 118 Robert Mugabe Avenue, in Windhoek's city centre, with a gallery, cinema theatre, classrooms and a restaurant.
The centre's about page says it was inaugurated on 30 January 1991. A memorial page for Sam Nujoma on the same site says Nujoma signed the creation of the centre on 31 July 1991.
Presidents Sam Nujoma and Jacques Chirac laid the foundation stone of the current building on 25 June 1998. Nujoma attended its official opening on 1 December 2000 (FNCC memorial page).
funding_verdict: Franco-Namibian Cultural Centre: state-funded by France: a binational body under Namibian law paid for by the French government

name: Huis Van Zessen
overview: Dike house at West Kinderdijk 89 in Alblasserdam, reached by Waterbus from the Erasmus Bridge in Rotterdam (house site).
Cornelis van Eesteren designed it in 1923 for the widow of the grocer Arie van Zessen, and his father's contracting firm built it (EFL Stichting).
Named for the Van Zessen family. Theo van Doesburg chose the colour scheme while Van Eesteren was in Paris (EFL Stichting).
funding_verdict: Huis Van Zessen: privately held: owned by EFL Stichting, which has investment income, with upkeep paid from visitors' voluntary contributions
